reference.source: WHO Classification of Skin Tumours / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A common benign dermal fibrohistiocytic proliferation, most often on the lower limbs of young to middle-aged women
It presents as a firm, well-defined papule or nodule, frequently with overlying brownish pigmentation
The dimple or Fitzpatrick sign, in which lateral pinching produces central dimpling, is a useful bedside clue
A history of preceding minor trauma or an insect bite is often reported, and its exact reactive versus neoplastic nature remains debated
Histology shows spindled fibroblasts and histiocytes in a storiform pattern with peripheral collagen trapping and overlying epidermal hyperplasia with basal hyperpigmentation
It is factor XIIIa positive and CD34 negative, the reverse of the profile of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Most lesions are stable and asymptomatic and require only reassurance, with excision reserved for diagnostic doubt or symptoms
Cellular, aneurysmal, and atypical variants exist and may occasionally recur locally after incomplete excision
reference.pathophysiology: Dermatofibroma is a benign proliferation of fibroblastic and histiocytic cells confined largely to the dermis, with some lesions extending into the superficial subcutis. The cells are arranged in a characteristic storiform, or cartwheel, pattern and characteristically entrap thickened collagen bundles at the periphery of the lesion. The overlying epidermis typically shows acanthosis with hyperpigmentation of the basal layer and sometimes induction of hair follicle-like or basaloid structures, producing the clinically apparent surface pigmentation. There is longstanding debate as to whether the lesion is a true clonal neoplasm or a reactive fibrosing response, often to minor trauma or an arthropod bite, and evidence exists on both sides. The immunophenotype, with expression of factor XIIIa and absence of CD34, is diagnostically important because it is the mirror image of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans and helps separate these two entities.
additionalDifferentials: Melanocytic naevus or, when pigmented, melanoma
Basal cell carcinoma when on sun-exposed skin
Cellular or atypical fibrous histiocytoma variants
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination including the dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign
Dermoscopy showing a central white scar-like patch with a peripheral pigment network
Excisional or punch biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain
Histology demonstrating storiform spindle cells with collagen trapping
Immunohistochemistry for factor XIIIa and CD34 to distinguish from dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Clinical follow-up of any lesion with atypical or changing features
redFlags: Rapid growth, large size, or a deep or fixed component suggesting dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Ulceration, bleeding, or marked change in a pigmented lesion raising concern for melanoma
Recurrence after excision, particularly with cellular or atypical variants
Multiple eruptive dermatofibromas, which may be associated with immunosuppression or autoimmune disease
reference.prognosis: Dermatofibroma is benign with an excellent prognosis and most lesions remain stable indefinitely, requiring no treatment. Cellular, aneurysmal, and atypical variants have a small risk of local recurrence but essentially no metastatic potential.
pitfalls: Mistaking a firm pigmented nodule for a melanoma, or vice versa, without dermoscopy or histology
Failing to distinguish dermatofibroma from dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, which needs wide excision
Overlooking multiple eruptive lesions as a marker of underlying immunosuppression
Assuming all fibrohistiocytic variants are equally indolent and neglecting follow-up of atypical forms
management: Reassure and observe, as typical asymptomatic lesions are benign and require no treatment
Confirm the diagnosis clinically with the dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign and dermoscopy, reserving biopsy for atypical or changing lesions
Offer surgical excision for symptomatic, diagnostically uncertain or cosmetically troublesome lesions
Use immunohistochemistry (factor XIIIa positive, CD34 negative) to distinguish it from dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans when uncertain
Monitor cellular, aneurysmal and atypical variants for local recurrence after excision
Follow up any lesion with atypical or evolving features clinically
